# Ectopic pregnancy

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Gynecologic surgery > Ectopic pregnancy*

[Original Article Link](/library/fO0k7T)

---

## Summary

<u>Ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u> occurs when an embryo attaches outside the <u>uterine cavity</u>, most commonly in the <u>fallopian tubes</u>. <u>Risk factors</u> include conditions that alter the anatomy of the <u>fallopian tubes</u> (e.g., history of <u>pelvic inflammatory disease</u>, previous <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u>, tubal <u>surgery</u>) and nonanatomical factors (e.g., smoking, age > 35 years, <u>assisted reproductive technology</u>). <u>Ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u> most commonly manifests 6–8 weeks after the <u>last menstrual period</u> and should be considered in individuals who can become pregnant and who have abdominal <u>pain</u> and <u>vaginal bleeding</u>. The first diagnostic step is a serum quantitative <u>β-hCG</u> test and <u>transvaginal ultrasound</u> (<u>TVUS</u>) to determine <u>pregnancy</u> location. Serial <u>β-hCG</u> tests and <u>TVUS</u> are frequently necessary to establish the diagnosis. Management in stable patients consists of <u>methotrexate</u>, <u>surgery</u> (e.g., <u>salpingostomy</u>, <u>salpingectomy</u>), or, in selected patients, <u>expectant management</u>. <u>Tubal rupture</u> due to <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u> manifests with severe abdominal <u>pain</u> and/or <u>acute abdomen</u>, signs of <u>peritoneal</u> irritation (e.g., shoulder <u>pain</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>), and sometimes signs of <u>hemodynamic instability</u> or <u>shock</u> (e.g., <u>hypotension</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, <u>syncope</u>). Patients with signs of <u>tubal rupture</u> require immediate stabilization and emergency <u>surgery</u>.

---

## Definitions

* <u>Ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u>: a <u>pregnancy</u> in which the fertilized egg attaches in a location outside the <u>uterine cavity</u>

* Tubal pregnancy: a <u>pregnancy</u> that occurs within the <u>fallopian tube</u> [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)

* Interstitial pregnancy: a <u>pregnancy</u> that occurs within the <u>interstitial</u> portion of the <u>fallopian tube</u> (i.e., the segment that connects the tube to the <u>endometrial</u> cavity)

* Cornual pregnancy: a <u>pregnancy</u> that occurs in the <u>uterine cornua</u>  [[2]](/library/qXVC_G0)[[3]](/library/DgV1xF0)

* Cesarean <u>scar</u> <u>pregnancy</u>: a <u>pregnancy</u> that occurs in the uterine <u>myometrium</u> at the site of a <u>cesarean delivery</u> <u>scar</u> [[4]](/library/3cVSXt0)

* Complicated ectopic pregnancy [[5]](/library/ribfGt)

* An <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u> with severe bleeding (e.g., <u>hemoperitoneum</u>, <u>vaginal bleeding</u>), rupture (e.g., <u>tubal rupture</u>), and/or hemodynamic compromise

* Gynecological emergency that requires surgical treatment

* Uncomplicated ectopic pregnancy [[5]](/library/ribfGt)

* An <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u> without any features of <u>complicated ectopic pregnancy</u>

* May resolve spontaneously

* Heterotopic pregnancy: a rare condition involving <u>multiple gestations</u>, in which one is intrauterine and another is <u>ectopic</u>; occurs more frequently in patients undergoing <u>infertility</u> treatments (e.g., <u>in vitro fertilization</u>)  [[6]](/library/MTcMrb0)

---

## Etiology

### Localization [[7]](/library/5F0ii3)




* <u>Fallopian tube</u> (∼ 95% of cases)

* Ampulla (∼ 70%)

* <u>Isthmus</u> (∼ 12%)

* <u>Fimbriae</u> (∼ 11%)

* <u>Interstitial</u> (∼ 2%)

* Other

* <u>Ovary</u>

* Cesarean <u>scar</u>[[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)

* Abdomen

* <u>Cervix</u>

* <u>Uterine cornua</u>





![Uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries](media/hsji3obsnsh0egn8ezwfbclh.jpg)

Uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries

![Sites of ectopic pregnancy](media/g8n7amhiflpkiqmyy5r03rii.jpg)

Sites of ectopic pregnancy




### Risk factors for ectopic pregnancy [[8]](/library/LgcwDb0)




Half of individuals with <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u> have no <u>risk factors</u>. [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)




#### <u>Anatomic alteration of the fallopian tubes</u>




* History of <u>PID</u> (e.g., <u>salpingitis</u>)

* Previous <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u>

* Surgeries involving the <u>fallopian tubes</u> (e.g. tubectomy, <u>tubal ligation</u>)

* <u>Endometriosis</u>

* <u>Ruptured appendix</u>  [[9]](/library/4cV3ct0)

* <u>Kartagener syndrome</u>

* Exposure to <u>diethylstilbestrol</u> (<u>DES</u>) in utero  [[10]](/library/nF07i3)[[11]](/library/LF0wi3)

* <u>Bicornuate uterus</u>





#### Nonanatomical <u>risk factors</u>




* Smoking

* Age > 35 years

* <u>Pregnancy</u> with <u>intrauterine device</u> in place   [[8]](/library/LgcwDb0)

* <u>Infertility</u>

* <u>In vitro fertilization</u>

---

## Clinical features

### General symptoms [[12]](/library/7F04j3)[[13]](/library/HF0Kj3)[[14]](/library/CCaq85)




Patients usually present with signs and symptoms 6–8 weeks after their <u>last menstrual period</u>.




* Lower abdominal <u>pain</u> and guarding (<u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u> is often mistaken for <u>appendicitis</u> due to the similarity of symptoms)

* <u>Vaginal bleeding</u>

* Signs of <u>pregnancy</u> 

* <u>Amenorrhea</u>

* <u>Nausea</u>

* <u>Breast</u> tenderness

* Frequent <u>urination</u>

* Tenderness or painful mass in the area of the <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u>

* <u>Cervical motion tenderness</u>, closed <u>cervix</u>

* <u>Interstitial pregnancies</u> tend to present late, at 7–12 weeks' <u>gestation</u>, because of myometrial distensibility.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Right lower quadrant</u> <u>pain</u> may indicate <u>appendicitis</u>. <u>Cervical motion tenderness</u> may be a sign of <u>PID</u>.




### Tubal rupture [[12]](/library/7F04j3)[[13]](/library/HF0Kj3)[[14]](/library/CCaq85)




* Acute course with sudden and severe lower abdominal <u>pain</u> (<u>acute abdomen</u>)

* Signs of <u>hemorrhagic shock</u> (e.g., <u>tachycardia</u>, <u>hypotension</u>, <u>syncope</u>)

* Features of <u>peritoneal</u> irritation (e.g., shoulder <u>pain</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>, urinary symptoms) due to bleeding [[8]](/library/LgcwDb0)

* More common in <u>interstitial pregnancy</u>

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach  [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)[[15]](/library/5Tcirb0)




Consider <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u> in all individuals who can become pregnant who present with general symptoms of <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u>, and in pregnant individuals with known <u>risk factors for ectopic pregnancy</u> in whom <u>pregnancy</u> location is unknown.




* <u>Hemodynamically unstable</u> patients

* Start acute stabilization measures (see “<u>Management of ruptured ectopic pregnancy</u>”).

* If trained, perform a <u>point-of-care ultrasound</u> (see “<u>POCUS in early pregnancy</u>” and “<u>FAST</u>”) to identify <u>intraperitoneal</u> free fluid or confirm <u>intrauterine pregnancy</u> (<u>IUP</u>).

* If <u>IUP</u> is confirmed, evaluate for alternate causes of <u>hemodynamic instability</u> (see “<u>Shock</u>”).

* If any of the following are present, refer for immediate surgical exploration without awaiting further diagnostic studies:

* Free <u>intraperitoneal</u> fluid

* Findings suggestive of <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u>, e.g., <u>adnexal mass</u>

* No visible <u>IUP</u> (if there is high clinical suspicion for <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u>)

* Urgently consult <u>OB/GYN</u> for surgical exploration based on clinical suspicion supplemented by <u>POCUS</u> findings (if performed).

* Obtain a <u>formal ultrasound</u> (<u>transvaginal ultrasound</u>) as soon as the patient is stable enough.

* Stable patients: Send serum <u>β-hCG</u> and arrange or perform a <u>pelvic</u> <u>ultrasound</u> (e.g., <u>POCUS for early pregnancy</u> or <u>formal ultrasound</u>) regardless of <u>β-hCG</u> level. [[15]](/library/5Tcirb0)

* <u>Ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u> visible on imaging (diagnosis confirmed): Begin treatment.

* <u>IUP</u> visible on imaging (<u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u> unlikely): Consider alternative diagnoses.

* Indeterminant <u>ultrasound</u> (<u>pregnancy of unknown location</u>) [[16]](/library/41V3St0)

* Arrange follow-up, serial <u>β-hCG</u>, and repeat imaging.

* <u>Undesired pregnancy</u>: Consider diagnostic <u>uterine aspiration</u> or <u>medical abortion</u> followed by serial <u>β-hCG</u> measurements.  [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)[[8]](/library/LgcwDb0)





> [!TIP]
> Sexually active individuals who can become pregnant and who present with abdominal <u>pain</u> and/or <u>vaginal bleeding</u> should undergo a <u>pregnancy test</u>, regardless of <u>contraception</u> use. [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)




> [!WARNING]
> Up to 20% of patients with <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u> can be <u>hemodynamically unstable</u> and require immediate therapy. Do not delay stabilization and definitive treatment to confirm the diagnosis! [[17]](/library/35YSPp)




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)[[8]](/library/LgcwDb0)[[18]](/library/KibUst)




#### Serum <u>β-hCG</u> level




* Single <u>β-hCG</u> measurement

* Increased <u>β-hCG</u> is verifiable from the eighth day after <u>ovulation</u>, when <u>fertilization</u> has occurred. [[8]](/library/LgcwDb0)

* A single measurement cannot be used to determine viability or <u>pregnancy</u> location. [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)[[19]](/library/CodqVI0)

* β-hCG discriminatory level: the <u>β-hCG</u> level at which an <u>IUP</u> is typically visible on <u>ultrasound</u>  [[15]](/library/5Tcirb0)

* Cutoffs for <u>transvaginal ultrasound</u> range from 1,500–3,500 mIU/mL <u>β-hCG</u>.  [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)[[8]](/library/LgcwDb0)

* Inability to visualize <u>pregnancy</u> on <u>ultrasound</u> above the <u>β-hCG</u> discriminatory level may suggest <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u> or <u>pregnancy loss</u>.

* <u>Multiple pregnancies</u> may have higher <u>β-hCG</u> levels.

* Serial β-hCG measurements (every 48 hours): better diagnostic <u>accuracy</u> than a single <u>β-hCG</u> level in differentiating <u>IUP</u> from <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u> [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)[[8]](/library/LgcwDb0)

* The expected percentage increase in <u>β-hCG</u> after 48 hours for normal IUPs is based on the initial level. 

* Initial level < 1,500 mIU/mL: > 49% expected increase

* Initial level 1,500–3,000 mIU/mL: > 40% expected increase

* Initial level > 3,000 mIU/mL: > 33% expected increase

* A lower than expected increase or any decline in <u>β-hCG</u> may indicate a failed <u>IUP</u> (e.g., <u>spontaneous abortion</u>) or an <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u>.

* A drop of ≥ 21% suggests failed <u>IUP</u>.

* A drop of < 21% is more likely to indicate an <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u>.

* An insufficient decline in serial <u>β-hCG</u> measurements following <u>induced abortion</u> should raise suspicion for <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u> (for more information, see “<u>Induced abortion</u>”).[[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)





> [!TIP]
> The <u>β-hCG discriminatory level</u> has limited <u>accuracy</u> and should not be used as the sole parameter to diagnose the location or viability of a <u>pregnancy</u>. Assessing trends on <u>serial β-hCG monitoring</u> is recommended instead. [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)[[15]](/library/5Tcirb0)




#### Additional studies




* <u>CBC</u>: <u>Anemia</u> may be seen in patients with <u>vaginal bleeding</u>.

* Blood <u>type and screen</u>: ABO and Rh testing to identify patients who might need Rho <u>immunization</u>

* <u>LFT</u>, <u>BMP</u>: to determine baseline <u>liver</u> and renal function





### Imaging [[8]](/library/LgcwDb0)[[20]](/library/nud7770)[[21]](/library/QbbutH)




#### <u>Transvaginal ultrasound</u> (<u>TVUS</u>)




Can be performed as a <u>formal ultrasound</u> or <u>POCUS for early pregnancy</u>.  [[22]](/library/nSc7ZX0)




* Indication: best initial imaging test for determining the location of the <u>pregnancy</u>

* Ultrasound findings suggestive of ectopic pregnancy

* Empty <u>uterine cavity</u> in combination with a thickened <u>endometrial</u> lining

* Possible free fluid within the <u>pouch of Douglas</u> (nonspecific)

* Additional findings in <u>tubal pregnancy</u>

* Possible extraovarian <u>adnexal mass</u>

* Tubal ring sign (<u>blob sign</u>): an echogenic ring that surrounds an unruptured <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u>   [[23]](/library/01Ye2L)

* Additional findings in <u>interstitial pregnancy</u> 

* Interstitial line sign: an echogenic line that extends from the <u>gestational sac</u> into the upper <u>uterus</u> (thought to be the echogenic appearance of the <u>interstitial</u> portion of the tube)

* A thin myometrial layer ( < 5 mm) surrounding the <u>gestational sac</u>

* Additional considerations

* <u>Ultrasound findings in normal pregnancy</u>: An <u>IUP</u> (i.e., a <u>gestational sac</u> and <u>yolk sac</u>, or embryo or fetus with cardiac activity in the <u>uterus</u>) typically becomes visible at 5–6 weeks' <u>gestation</u>. [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)[[15]](/library/5Tcirb0)

* If the <u>gestational sac</u> cannot be seen at all on <u>ultrasound</u>, the patient is diagnosed with pregnancy of unknown location. [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)





![Tubal ring sign (blob sign) of ectopic pregnancy](media/kzxqmbwlv4nqoodopxy20mpq.jpg)

Tubal ring sign (blob sign) of ectopic pregnancy

![Ectopic pregnancy](media/zp9qq3s2fadhb8pkn4f7p5ci.jpg)

Ectopic pregnancy




#### Transabdominal <u>ultrasound</u> (TAUS)




* Can be used to exclude differential diagnoses (e.g., <u>acute appendicitis</u>)

* Provides a general picture of the <u>pelvic</u> anatomy and upper abdomen but is less sensitive than <u>TVUS</u> in detecting extrauterine <u>pregnancy</u>

* <u>POCUS</u> can be performed using the transabdominal approach to rapidly rule in <u>IUP</u> if present.





![Ectopic pregnancy](media/cq7le16q2tsahv5sgstf8815.jpg)

Ectopic pregnancy




### <u>Uterine aspiration</u> [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)[[8]](/library/LgcwDb0)




* Indication: Consider in cases of <u>pregnancy of unknown location</u> when <u>pregnancy</u> is undesired or nonviability is certain.

* Findings on uterine <u>aspirate</u> examination [[24]](/library/c1Vaft0)

* <u>Ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u>: <u>decidualization</u> of the <u>endometrium</u> without <u>chorionic villi</u>

* <u>IUP</u>: <u>Chorionic villi</u> and <u>gestational sac</u> are present.





### <u>Exploratory laparoscopy</u> [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)



* Indications

* Unstable patients suspected of having an <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u>

* In <u>pregnancy of unknown location</u> if the location is still uncertain after 7–10 days




![Fallopian tube with an ectopic pregnancy](media/oj2qu7fqyx91l06wxlq19s8e.jpg)

Fallopian tube with an ectopic pregnancy




> [!WARNING]
> Do not delay <u>laparoscopy</u> in unstable patients with <u>suspected ectopic pregnancy</u>!

## Treatment

The following recommendations are consistent with the 2018 (reaffirmed 2025) <u>ACOG</u> practice bulletin on tubal <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u>. [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)




### Approach




* Unstable patients: See “<u>Management of ruptured ectopic pregnancy</u>.”

* Begin acute stabilization.

* Obtain an immediate <u>OB/GYN</u> consult for emergency <u>surgery</u>.

* Stable patients: Determine whether medical, surgical, or <u>expectant management</u> is appropriate.

* Consider clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings.

* Share decision-making with patients in consultation with <u>OB/GYN</u>.

* Patients suited to medical or <u>expectant management</u> at home

* Provide education on <u>red flag symptoms</u> indicating rupture, e.g., severe worsening <u>pain</u>, shoulder tip <u>pain</u>, <u>dizziness</u>, or heavy bleeding.

* Arrange appropriate follow-up prior to discharge.

* All patients: Provide <u>supportive care</u>.

* <u>Pain management</u>

* Prenatal and <u>contraceptive</u> counseling once treatment is complete  [[25]](/library/-dcDsY0)

* <u>Anti-D</u> <u>immunoglobulin</u> for <u>Rh-negative</u> patients  (for more information see “<u>Dosages of RhIG</u>”)  [[26]](/library/nfW75k0)





> [!WARNING]
> Do not forget <u>anti-D immunoglobulin</u> in all <u>Rh-negative</u> patients with bleeding!




### Medical therapy (<u>methotrexate</u>) [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)[[8]](/library/LgcwDb0)




<u>MTX</u> is the treatment of choice.




* Mechanism of action: inhibits <u>folate</u>-dependent steps in <u>DNA synthesis</u> to terminate the rapidly dividing <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u>.

* Indications 

* <u>Uncomplicated ectopic pregnancies</u>

* Hemodynamically stable patients

* Unruptured mass < 4 cm on <u>TVUS</u> [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)

* No fetal heartbeat

* <u>Absolute contraindications</u>

* Chronic conditions

* Pulmonary (except <u>asthma</u>)

* Renal (e.g., <u>creatinine clearance</u> < 50 mL/min/1.73 m<sup>2</sup>)

* Hepatic (e.g., <u>alcohol use disorder</u>, <u>chronic liver disease</u>) [[8]](/library/LgcwDb0)

* Hematologic (e.g., <u>leukopenia</u>, <u>thrombocytopenia</u>, <u>severe anemia</u>)

* <u>IUP</u>

* <u>Breastfeeding</u>

* <u>MTX</u> <u>sensitivity</u>

* <u>Immunodeficiency</u>

* <u>Peptic ulcer disease</u>

* <u>Ruptured ectopic pregnancy</u>

* Unable to engage in follow-up

* Administration: Regimen is determined by <u>ultrasound</u> and clinical findings, patient preferences, and <u>β-hCG</u> level.  [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)[[8]](/library/LgcwDb0)

* <u>β-hCG</u> < 3,600 mIU/mL: single-dose regimen

* <u>β-hCG</u> 3,600–5,000 mIU/mL: Consider two-dose regimen.





| <br>Methotrexate regimens for medical treatment of ectopic pregnancy [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Single-dose regimen | Two-dose regimen | Multiple-dose regimen |
| Characteristics | <br>* Lower risk of adverse effects than other regimens<br><br> | <br>* More effective than single-dose regimen for patients with high initial <u>β-hCG</u><br><br> | <br><br>* More adverse effects than other regimens<br><br>* Higher success rate than other available regimens<br><br><br> |
| Administration | <br>* Day 1: <u>methotrexate</u> DOSAGE<br><br> | <br><br>* Day 1: <u>methotrexate</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* Day 4: <u>methotrexate</u> DOSAGE<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Days 1, 3, 5, 7: <u>methotrexate</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* Days 2, 4, 6, 8: <u>leucovorin</u> DOSAGE<br><br><br> |
| <u>β-hCG</u> monitoring | <br><br>* <u>β-hCG</u> on day 4<br><br>* <u>β-hCG</u> on day 7<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>β-hCG</u> on day 4 (after treatment)<br><br>* <u>β-hCG</u> on day 7<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>β-hCG</u> on days of treatment with <u>MTX</u><br><br> |
| Response to <u>β-hCG</u> monitoring results | <br><br>* Decrease > 15% from day 4 to day 7: Measure <u>β-hCG</u> weekly until negative.<br><br>* Decrease < 15% from day 4 to day 7: Repeat <u>MTX</u> dose.<br><br>* No decrease after 2 doses: Consider surgical management.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Decrease > 15% from day 4 to day 7: Measure <u>β-hCG</u> weekly until negative.<br><br>* Decrease < 15% from day 4 to day 7: Repeat <u>MTX</u> dose on day 7 and measure <u>β-hCG</u> on day 11.<br><br>* This may be repeated until the patient has received 4 doses.<br><br>* No decrease after 4 doses: Consider surgical management.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Decrease > 15% in 2 consecutive measurements: Discontinue <u>MTX</u> and measure <u>β-hCG</u> weekly until negative.<br><br>* No <u>β-hCG</u> decrease after 4 doses: Consider surgical management.<br><br><br> |
| Follow up | <br>* If <u>β-hCG</u> levels increase or plateau during weekly follow up, consider persistent <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u>.<br><br> |  |  |





* Adverse effects: See “<u>Adverse effects of immunosuppressants</u>.”

* Patients should avoid the following during <u>MTX</u> therapy:

* Exercise and <u>sexual activity</u>

* <u>Folic acid</u> supplements, foods with a high <u>folic acid</u> content, and <u>NSAIDs</u>

* Prolonged exposure to sunlight

* <u>Alcohol</u> and gas-producing foods





> [!WARNING]
> <u>MTX</u> therapy is contraindicated in <u>ruptured ectopic pregnancy</u>!




### Nonurgent surgical management [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)[[8]](/library/LgcwDb0)




See “<u>Management of ruptured ectopic pregnancy</u>” for emergency surgical indications and preferred approach.




* Indications for nonurgent <u>surgery</u>

* Contraindications for <u>MTX</u>

* Unsuccessful medical treatment

* A concurrent surgical procedure (e.g., bilateral tubal blockage) is necessary.

* The patient has indicated a preference for surgical treatment.

* Approach <u>Laparoscopy</u> (preferred)

* Procedure: salpingostomy, i.e., removal of <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u> without removing the affected <u>fallopian tube</u> (tube‑conserving operation)

* Preferred in patients with unruptured <u>tubal pregnancy</u> who do not meet the criteria for <u>conservative treatment</u>

* Complications

* Risk of persistent <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u>

* Risk of repeat <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u>

* Additional considerations

* Patients require serial <u>hCG</u> measurement.

* Consider a prophylactic dose of <u>MTX</u> if there is concern for incomplete resection.

* <u>Salpingectomy</u> may be required in select cases (e.g., large <u>ectopic</u> mass).





![Tubal pregnancy](media/g67g8jskwgq0hsk2jsmfz9oh.jpg)

Tubal pregnancy




### <u>Expectant management</u> [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)




Asymptomatic patients with very low <u>β-hCG</u> levels may experience spontaneous resolution of <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u> without medical or surgical treatment. Consider this approach in select patients after consultation with <u>OB/GYN</u>.  [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)




* Indications

* Minimal symptoms

* No evidence of <u>ectopic</u> mass on <u>TVUS</u>

* Confirmed plateauing or decreasing serial <u>β-hCG</u> levels

* Considerations during <u>expectant management</u>

* Provide extensive counseling on the risks of complications in addition to general counseling (see “Approach”).

* Arrange close surveillance and serial <u>β-hCG</u> measurement (e.g., every 2–7 days).

* Conversion to medical or surgical therapy

* Increasing symptoms, e.g., <u>pain</u>, signs of <u>ruptured ectopic pregnancy</u>

* Insufficient decrease, persistent plateau, or increase in <u>β-hCG</u> levels

---

## Ruptured ectopic pregnancy

Follow the <u>ABCDE approach</u> for patients with obvious signs of rupture and those at high risk of impending rupture.




### Rapid assessment




Suspect <u>ruptured ectopic pregnancy</u> in patients in their <u>first trimester</u> with any of the following:




* <u>Clinical features of shock</u>: e.g., <u>tachycardia</u>, <u>hypotension</u>, <u>pallor</u>

* Severe abdominal or <u>pelvic pain</u>

* <u>Peritoneal signs</u> on examination

* Significant <u>vaginal bleeding</u>

* <u>POCUS</u> positive for <u>intraperitoneal</u> free fluid

* Clinical deterioration after receiving <u>MTX</u> therapy [[15]](/library/5Tcirb0)

![AMBOSS POCUS series | Free fluid in splenorenal recess](media/small_61f95cd405e80.jpg)

AMBOSS POCUS series | Free fluid in splenorenal recess




> [!WARNING]
> Obtain emergency <u>OB/GYN</u> consult without delay if <u>ruptured ectopic pregnancy</u> is likely!




### Acute stabilization




* <u>Obtain IV access</u>; send an urgent <u>type and screen</u> and <u>crossmatch</u>.

* Start immediate <u>IV fluid resuscitation</u>.

* Rapidly deliver <u>blood transfusion</u> as soon as <u>blood products</u> are available.

* Activate <u>massive transfusion</u> protocol if necessary.

* Consider <u>tranexamic acid</u> DOSAGE for persistently unstable patients in consultation with OBGYN.  [[27]](/library/wdchHY0)[[28]](/library/Thc6WX0)[[29]](/library/ShcyWX0)

* If <u>hypotension</u> persists, start <u>vasopressors</u> (see “<u>Shock</u>”).

* Consider interventional radiology referral for <u>angioembolization</u> in consultation with <u>OB/GYN</u>.





### Surgical management




* Indications for immediate surgical referral

* <u>Hemodynamic instability</u>

* Symptoms of impending rupture (e.g., severe <u>pelvic pain</u>)

* Signs of <u>intraperitoneal</u> bleeding (e.g., <u>peritonitis</u>, <u>POCUS</u> positive for free fluid)

* Extrauterine embryo with cardiac activity seen on <u>ultrasound</u> [[8]](/library/LgcwDb0)

* <u>Risk factors</u> for rupture  [[30]](/library/a80QO3)

* Approach: <u>Laparotomy</u> is preferred for large <u>intraperitoneal</u> bleeding or critically unstable patients; otherwise a <u>laparoscopic</u> approach is typically performed.

* Procedure: salpingectomy, i.e., partial or complete removal of the affected <u>fallopian tube</u> (does not preserve tube function)

* Preferred approach for:

* Ruptured tube

* Heavy bleeding

* Large <u>ectopic</u> mass

* Severe damage to the <u>fallopian tube</u>

* Additional considerations

* If the patient desires future <u>pregnancies</u>: Evaluate the status of the <u>contralateral</u> <u>fallopian tube</u> before <u>salpingectomy</u>.

* If the patient does not desire future <u>pregnancies</u>: Bilateral <u>salpingectomy</u> may be performed.

---

## Prognosis

* The condition is fatal for the fetus.

* <u>Maternal mortality rate</u>: ∼ 0.6/100,000 in the US [[32]](/library/I4XYky)

* Future <u>fertility</u>: depends primarily on <u>fertility</u> status prior to <u>ectopic</u> <u>pregnancy</u>

* Recurrence: approx. 10% [[1]](/library/HMWKJN0)
